report_quotes: Ram Piari, an employee of Raj Kumari

source_evidence.quote: Ram Piari, who was the daughter of one Chandar Bit, an employee of Raj Kumari working in her tea estate.

serious_errors.materiality: The report converts Ram Piari from the employee’s daughter into Raj Kumari’s employee, changing a relationship relevant to the alleged marriage introduction and rival property-provenance narratives. The record does not establish that this misdescription altered the inheritance-priority analysis.

source_evidence.quote: the parties were governed by Hindu law

serious_errors.materiality: Recasting the High Court’s Hindu-law succession finding as a conflict with statutory Hindu law can alter the legal framing of custom’s applicability and priority. No particular historically applicable succession statute is supplied; a material wrong-law consequence is therefore not confirmed.

important_omissions: The report leaves out the independent family-conduct evidence that Paras Ram addressed the plaintiff as jija and that school records, filed by teacher Lala Bishan Das, identified Paras Ram as the plaintiff’s sala (S36a6c315daba; Sc0c5e8da1cee; Sc0c5e8da1cee). This bears on the marriage evidence beyond cohabitation and letters.

The High Court’s second Evidence Act section 50 objection is not stated: legally relevant relationship opinion must be expressed by conduct, not merely voiced, by persons with special means of knowledge (Sc073ce64d379; L6052a06ef1a9).

The report does not set out the plaintiff’s competing 1934–35 account that Raj Kumari took Ram Piari from his home, contrasting with Raj Kumari’s account of Ram Piari returning to Holta after years with the driver. This was a genuine conflict in narrative and potential credibility (S55b6c2be1fbc; S8e8de02b9c7c).

The defendants’ independent position that the alleged custom would not govern Ram Piari’s personal or self-acquired property, even apart from their denial that the appellant was governed by custom, is only indirectly reflected in the final conditional question (S68be74e96323; Sadbb580bf3ae).
main_answer_reason: The report substantively answers the scoped priority question by attributing the competing accounts of marriage and funding, tracing trial and High Court findings, distinguishing a cohabitation presumption from the High Court’s rebuttal assessment, identifying the property-specific rejection of husband-first custom, and withholding the unknown target appellate disposition. Two local defects—the misidentified employee relationship and unsupported “statutory” description—plus omissions of some corroborative and section 50 detail do not negate the main attributed conditional analysis; their effects are inventoried separately.
uncertainties: The target court’s final reasoning and disposition are withheld; none is inferred from the prior High Court findings.
Whether any historically applicable statutory succession rule governed the parties is not established by the supplied LAW excerpts or CASE references.
The exact year 1932 is an inference from “sometime in 1921” and “after about 11 years,” not an independently specified date.

The source excerpt referring to “Ram Hari’s own mother” and the excerpt identifying “Ram Piari’s own mother” have a naming/transcription inconsistency; the report’s contextual attribution to Ram Piari’s mother is supported without reconstructing further facts.
The precise legal significance of Ram Piari’s father working for Raj Kumari, beyond correcting the false statement that Ram Piari worked for her, cannot be determined from this view.
